newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Howzit, robot, jol - S.Africa gets own dictionary.
newsitem.headline: Howzit, robot, jol - S.Africa gets own dictionary.

text.p: South African English wins new academic respectability with the launch on Thursday of a very fat dictionary of its own. But lurking in its pages are unwelcome reminders of a far from respectable past.

The Oxford University Press has partly atoned for decades of foreign fun-poking at drawling South African vowels and unique terms such as braai for barbecue, howzit for hello-how-are-you? and robots for traffic lights.
But the vocabulary of racialism that most South Africans hope will soon be tagged "obsolete" or "archaic" crowd the Dictionary of South African English on Historical Principles.
"I've never seen so many references to racism," one shocked reviewer told the Johannesburg Star newspaper.
Kaffir, the most hated insult for a black person, fills eight and a half sides with unsavoury examples of how to use it.
"Offensive in all senses and combinations" the definition says for a word that in its original Arabic meant infidel.

There are insults for everyone else too, such as rockspider -- a creature that crawls out from under a stone -- or kaaskop (cheesehead) for the Dutch-origin Afrikaners who over four decades institutionalised and perfected racial segregation.
Their revenge term for the English, soutpiel (salty penis), has made it into English and the dictionary.
It sums up the disdain the "white African" tribe felt for rivals who still yearned for their Old Country and kept one foot in South Africa and the other in England, straddling the ocean.
There are in fact numerous variants of English in a country whose races were until recently forced by law to live apart.
"We were so divided by the Group Areas Act that English words in everyday use in the (black) townships were often unknown to other communities," the Star commented.
Only now are they starting slowly to merge into one dialect.

The 825-page, 5,000-entry reference work is the fullest ever record of how South Africans speak what is now just one of 11 official languages but is rapidly becoming their lingua franca. "There are vulgarisms and slang but much of what we take for granted as standard English was invented right here on African soil," said its South African managing editor, Penny Silva.
Commando, trek and even satyagraha -- Mahatma Gandhi's philosophy of truth and perserverance -- are all terms that entered English through South Africa.
Concentration camp -- a British invention from the Anglo- Boer war at the turn of the century -- is said to be another.

The book can almost be read as a history of South Africa, particularly the recent era of turbulent struggle against racial segregation or apartheid, an Afrikaner word for separateness that has passed into the languages of the world.
"Apartheid terminology is fully documented, clearly marked as historical if appropriate and with clear warnings as to the offensive and derogatory nature of the words," the editors note.

Researchers began work a quarter-century ago when gardeners and maids were patronisingly called boys and girls, immorality meant sex between races and non-European meant sub-human -- except for "honorary whites" such as visiting Asian businessmen.

They kept adding newly coined political terms such as bantustan -- a disparaging term for so-called independent homelands for blacks -- or necklacing, the horrific burning-tyre death that awaited black collaborators.
One of the last entries to scrape in was the new meaning Archbishop Desmond Tutu gave to the word rainbow of multiracial or multicultural -- as in "the rainbow nation".
Boer and veld, borrowed Dutch words for farmer and field that were adapted to South Africa, are among the oldest, dating back to the first settlers' arrival in the 1600s and 1700s.
"We've got nearly 5,000 words which are specific to South Africa," said Silva.

Borrowings have flooded in from the Dutch off-shoot Afrikaans and from the immigrants and locals who make up modern South Africa -- the Khoisan (Bushmen and Hottentots), Zulus, Xhosa, Malays, Indians, Jews, Portuguese and even Japanese.
Most local words deal not with politics, but everyday life -- including a liberal sprinkling of recreation terms from jol (pronounced jawl) for a wild party to dagga for marijuana.
Some have taken on new meanings such as taxi for minibus, tearoom for cafe and cafe for corner shop.
And, to frustrate foreigners, "just now" means "not quite now, but soon enough".
